extracted.intended_audience: power sector stakeholders (utilities, plant owners/operators), state regulators, EPA reviewers, environmental and industry commenters, and technical/legal analysts of EPA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: BSER determination for fossil fuel EGUs
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidentiary criteria used by EPA to determine the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units, including evaluation of CCS, natural gas co-firing, and highly efficient generation plus operational practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS as a multi-component technology (capture, transportation, sequestration/storage)
rubrics_metrics.description: CCS has three major components: CO2 capture, transportation, and sequestration/storage. Solvent-based CO2 capture has long industrial history and CCS includes capture systems, pipelines, and sequestration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate CCS as an integrative system (not just capture). Use historical industrial experience (e.g., solvent capture patents, thousands of miles of CO2 pipelines, tens of millions of tons permanently stored) and specific project examples to assess whether CCS is a practicable BSER component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrated performance and commercial readiness of CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether CCS is a 'proven technology' and commercially deployable at scale, supported by prior pilot, demonstration, and full-scale projects and industry statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider documented deployments (e.g., Petra Nova, Boundary Dam), industry views (API: 'CCS is a proven technology'), pilot and demonstration outcomes, and existence of operating projects and those in advanced development (at least 15 operating and 121 under construction/advanced development cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost trends and cost-effectiveness (including policy incentives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recent decreases in CCS and co-firing costs—and the effects of incentives like the IRA and IRC section 45Q tax credits—are central to judging whether technologies are cost-effective as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use techno-economic analyses and observed cost declines (e.g., projected 50% fall in capture cost from coal-fired generation by 2025 relative to 2010). Account for tax credits (e.g., 45Q increases under the IRA) and project-specific FEED studies and vendor claims when evaluating cost-effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to meet specific emissions performance levels (capture percentage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a technology can achieve specified emission reduction levels (e.g., EPA references a 90 percent capture amine-based BSER and cites projects targeting >97 percent capture).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess measured or modeled capture rates from deployed or planned projects (amine-based systems, Allam-Fetvedt cycle, NET Power) and whether those rates meet the emission reduction requirements used in the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infrastructure readiness (pipelines and storage capacity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Availability of CO2 transport and sequestration infrastructure (e.g., 'thousands of miles of CO2 pipelines' and tens of millions of tons stored) that enables deployment at scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate existing pipeline networks, sequestration sites, and planned infrastructure expansions; consider whether required transport and storage can be practically and timely developed for affected units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project pipeline and timing (operating projects, FEED studies, construction schedules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence and schedule of operating, under-construction, FEED-completed, and advanced-development projects that indicate feasibility ahead of regulatory compliance dates (examples: projects expected to be built and operational before Jan 1, 2032).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence of FEED completions, pilot projects, and announced commercial projects (e.g., Project Tundra, Coal Creek, NET Power projects) to judge likely deployment timing relative to compliance deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: State policy and regulatory environment as a deployment driver
rubrics_metrics.description: State mandates, incentives, or targets (e.g., North Dakota carbon-neutral goals, Wyoming SB 42 requiring CCS-equipped coal generation) materially affect the feasibility and expected deployment of technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In assessing BSER feasibility and nationwide applicability, account for state laws, utility IRPs, and state-level incentives or mandates that make technology deployment more likely in certain jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural gas co-firing technical feasibility for coal-fired steam units
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural gas co-firing involves substituting gas for some coal; existing boilers can be modified (new gas burners, pipeline connections) and many units already have multi-fuel capability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical and reported co-firing practice (e.g., 249 of 565 coal-fired units reported natural gas use; 29 units co-fired >=60% hourly), required boiler modifications, pipeline availability, and documented examples of conversions when evaluating co-firing as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital and operational cost trends for natural gas co-firing
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs of co-firing have declined due to smaller coal/gas price differentials and lower capital costs for boiler modifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use recent cost analyses and the EPA's detailed reviews in technical support documents (TSDs/RIA) to evaluate cost-effectiveness and prevalence of co-firing modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highly efficient generation for new and reconstructed combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain new/reconstructed simple cycle and combined cycle combustion turbines, 'highly efficient generation' (thermal efficiency improvements) is identified as BSER to reduce CO2 per MWh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate manufacturer- and project-level demonstrated efficiencies; consider technical measures (increased firing temperature, higher pressure ratios, intercooling) and whether higher-efficiency turbines are commercially available and cost-effective for the affected source category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational and maintenance (O&M) best practices as part of BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with hardware/technology, 'best operating and maintenance practices' contribute to emissions reductions and are considered part of the BSER evaluation for combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include O&M measures (procedures, controls, maintenance regimes) in assessments of achievable emission reductions and consider documented evidence that O&M combined with efficient turbines reduces fuel consumption and emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of EGU roles, dispatch, capacity factor, and reliability constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: EGUs play different roles (base load, intermediate, peaking) and contribute to grid reliability (frequency/voltage regulation, black start, reserves); availability, dispatch order, outages, age, and capacity factor affect feasibility of retrofit/controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining BSER applicability and feasibility, examine unit-specific operational characteristics (capacity factor, outage frequency, role in the grid), regional transmission operator structures, and reliability obligations that may constrain or shape feasible control options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sector trends and projections influence on BSER feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term shifts (growing renewables and nuclear, projected zero-emitting share increases) and utility commitments can affect which technologies are reasonable to require as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate EPA power sector projections (e.g., Power Sector Platform 2023 projecting zero-emitting sources rising to 76% by 2040), corporate and state commitments, and retirement/conversion trends when judging whether BSER is pragmatic and cost-effective across affected units.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of climate and non-climate benefits (FrEDI and social cost of greenhouse gases)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses modeling frameworks (FrEDI) and monetizes emission reductions via the social cost of greenhouse gases to quantify climate-related damages and benefits of emission reductions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use peer-reviewed impact studies aggregated in models like FrEDI and apply SC-GHG estimates to monetize avoided damages; incorporate regional differences in impacts and note limitations (partial assessments, omitted interactions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of non-climate GHG impacts and co-benefits (air quality, health, ecosystems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some GHGs have direct non-climate impacts (CO2 effects on plant growth and ocean acidification; N2O ozone depletion; methane forming tropospheric ozone); climate change also affects air quality, wildfire smoke, and public health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include assessment of co-benefits and non-climate harms (health risks from increased ozone, smoke, vector-borne disease, infrastructure damages, and ecosystem losses) when weighing the overall benefits and justification for BSER options.
